summary:
Every room number is between 1 and n, so it also names a slot of the array (`room − 1`). That lets the
array itself record which rooms have been seen, either with a sign or by adding n per booking, so no
extra memory is needed. Adding n even keeps the answer in increasing order for free.

question.md:
`bookings` has n entries, each a room number from 1 to n, and no room appears more than twice. Return
the rooms that appear **exactly twice**, in increasing order.

- **Values 1 … n and length n:** every value is a valid index after subtracting 1. That's the
  property every clever approach here relies on.
- **At most twice** means "seen before" is enough to identify a double booking: there's never a third
  copy to worry about.
- **Sorted output**, even though the bookings come in any order.
- **The challenge:** O(n) time with O(1) extra space besides the answer. A count array would be O(n)
  extra space.

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- No room booked twice: return an empty list.
- Each room appears at most twice, so counts are 0, 1 or 2.
- The answer must be in increasing order.

think.md:
**The array as its own checklist.** When the values are numbers `1 … n` and the array has `n` slots, slot `v − 1` can
serve as the checkbox for value `v`. To tick it, change slot `v − 1` in a way that is **reversible** and that doesn't
destroy the value stored there:

- **Flip its sign** (values are positive, so the original is `|x|`);
- **Add `n`** (the original is `(x − 1) mod n + 1`, and the number of additions counts how often `v` appeared).

Reading a slot's value always uses the decoding (`abs`, or the `mod`), so earlier ticks never confuse later reads.
That's O(n) time with O(1) extra space, and a final pass can restore the input.

**Counting in place by adding `n`.** For each booking, decode the room `v = (x − 1) mod n + 1` (the original
value, even if `n` has been added to this slot), then add `n` to slot `v − 1`. Each slot ends at
`original + n · (times its room was booked)`. A room booked twice has gained `2n`, so its slot exceeds `2n`.
For `[5, 1, 4, 5, 2, 1, 7]` (n = 7):
Slots above 14: rooms **[1, 5]**. Decoding each slot with `(x − 1) mod n + 1` restores the input.

Rooms booked exactly twice, in increasing order.

approaches.title: Mark seen rooms with a minus sign

idea.md:
Read rooms with `|x|`. If slot `v − 1` is already negative, room `v` was seen before: it's double-booked.
Otherwise negate it. Restore the signs and sort the answer (rooms are found in input order).

build: For each booking, check the sign of its room's slot.

lines.text: The room number, ignoring any sign added by a mark.
Its slot is already negative: this is the room's second booking.
First booking of this room: tick its slot by negating it.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n)** because the answer is sorted (the marking itself is O(n)). **Space O(1)** besides the answer.

steps.text: Every value is a room 1 … n, so `value − 1` is a valid slot. A negative slot means 'that room was seen'.
Read 5 (index 0): slot 4 was positive. Flip it to mark room 5 as seen.
Read 1 (index 1): slot 0 was positive. Flip it to mark room 1 as seen.
Read 4 (index 2): slot 3 was positive. Flip it to mark room 4 as seen.
Read 5 (index 3): slot 4 is already negative, so room 5 was seen before. Twice!
Read 2 (index 4): slot 1 was positive. Flip it to mark room 2 as seen.
Read 1 (index 5): slot 0 is already negative, so room 1 was seen before. Twice!
Read 7 (index 6): slot 6 was positive. Flip it to mark room 7 as seen.
Found in reading order [5, 1]; sort to get [1, 5].

walk.title: Use the sign of slot v − 1 as a 'room v seen' flag. Meeting an already negative slot means a second booking.

limits.md: Rooms are discovered in input order, so the answer needs a sort. Counting by adding `n` lets a final left-to-right read produce them already sorted.

approaches.title: Count in place by adding n

idea.md:
Add `n` to slot `v − 1` for each booking (decoding `v` with `(x − 1) mod n + 1`). Then a left-to-right pass
reports every slot above `2n` and restores each value with the same decoding.

**Why `> 2n` means twice.** A slot starts between 1 and `n`; after `k` additions it lies in
`(k·n, (k + 1)·n]`. Only `k = 2` puts it above `2n`.

build: Read slots above `2n` in index order.

lines.text: Decode the room even if this slot has already been increased, then count the booking in its room's slot.
A slot that gained `2n` belongs to a room booked twice; reading by index gives increasing order.
Decoding with `(x − 1) mod n + 1` removes the added multiples of `n`.

complexity.md: **Time O(n).** **Space O(1)** besides the answer. Values reach at most `3n`, so there's no overflow.

steps.text: n = 7. Read each value as (value − 1) mod n + 1 so additions made earlier don't hide it.
Slots above 2n = 14 were bumped twice: rooms [1, 5], already in order. Then each slot is restored with (value − 1) mod n + 1.

walk.title: Add n to slot v − 1 for every booking of room v. Afterwards slot i holds original + n × (bookings of room i + 1).

takeaways.md:
- **Count in place:** add `n` per occurrence; decode with `(x − 1) mod n + 1`.
- Sign marks record "seen"; additions record "how many".
- **Pitfall:** reading a slot without decoding it after it has been marked.
